pedagogy.summary: Children learn to seriate three or more objects by length and to compare two objects that cannot be placed side by side by using a third object (a string or strip) as an intermediary. The reasoning underneath is transitivity: if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — and a portable copy of one length lets you carry a comparison across a gap.
bestPractices: Serial ordering: give three (then more) ribbons or cube-towers and encourage a strategy — pick the shortest, then the next shortest — rather than random trial-and-error.
Set a genuine problem where two objects cannot be moved together (a doorway vs a bookshelf) so the child discovers a string/strip as a portable copy of a length.
Voice the transitive inference explicitly: 'the door is taller than the string; the shelf is shorter than the string; so the door is taller than the shelf.'
Keep the intermediary constant — uncut, unstretched, aligned at the same end — because a re-cut or stretched string breaks the comparison; use it to build conservation of length.
Use insert-into-series tasks: 'where does this new ribbon go?' to push beyond trial-and-error toward a mental image of an increasing series.
keyRepresentations: A set of three-plus ribbons or cube-towers arranged as an increasing 'staircase'
A length of string or paper strip used as an intermediary copy of a length
The seriation staircase image (each step the smallest increase in length)
commonMisconceptions: Compares only pairs and never chains the inference — insists on placing A directly against C instead of reasoning through the intermediary.
Orders by trial-and-error with no image of an increasing series, and cannot say where a new object should be inserted.
Does not keep the intermediary constant — stretches, re-cuts, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons.
Non-conservation: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.

learn.summary: Children learn to seriate three or more objects by length and to compare two objects that cannot be placed side by side by using a third object (string or paper strip) as a fixed intermediary length. The underlying reasoning is transitivity: if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — and a string kept at one fixed length lets a comparison be carried across a gap. Enactive ordering and carrying an intermediary build the reasoning; recognition formats and static displays can check or summarise it.

activities.title: Carrying a length across a gap with a string
feedback: If the child says the objects 'can't be compared, they're too far apart' or tries to move one object to the other: model comparing the string to A, then to B, and voice 'A vs string, string vs B, so A vs B'; secure direct side-by-side comparison first so the string has a length to stand for.

If the child re-cuts, stretches, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons: emphasise the string must stay the same single length for both objects; mark its end and align the same starting point each time. (Setting the string to match one object's length at the start is fine — the rule is only that it must not change between comparisons.)

If the child says the string 'got shorter/longer' after it is bent or moved: treat this as a conservation stage, not carelessness — straighten-and-compare so the child sees the length is unchanged, and revisit later rather than correcting hard.

Probe: 'How do you know this one is taller if you never put them next to each other?' and 'If the string were longer than BOTH objects, could you still tell which is taller? How?' (This last case shows the need to compare how each object lines up against the string, not just a longer/shorter label.)
activities.rationale: Indirect comparison via a third object is a Grade 1/Year 2 measurement expectation, with the canonical task of judging which of two paths or objects is longer by laying one length of string along each (one longer than the string, the other shorter). Enacting the carry makes the transitive inference concrete; keeping the intermediary at one fixed length between comparisons develops conservation of length.
sourceClaims: The Transitivity Principle — if A is longer than B and B is longer than C then A is longer than C — is a Grade 1 expectation used for indirect comparison when direct comparison is impossible; the canonical example is judging which of two paths is longer via a length of string laid along each (one path longer than the string, the other shorter).

The Length Indirect Comparer compares two objects by representing them with a third object (e.g. a piece of string) and discussion focuses on transitive inference; a child at this level may use a ruler but often ignores the starting point. Serial Orderer levels: children first order 3–5 lengths by trial-and-error, then build a mental image of an increasing series and seriate by choosing the shortest then the 'smallest difference' next, and learn to insert a length by making it longer than those on one side and shorter than those on the other.
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths and heights and use indirect comparison / a third object to compare objects that cannot be placed together.
learnerActions: Face two objects (e.g. two cube-towers, or a tall object by the door and a shelf across the room) that are clearly too far apart to bring together and line up.

Hold a fixed length of string against the first object, aligned at the same starting end, and note whether that object is taller or shorter than the string; keep the string's length unchanged for both comparisons (do not change it between the two objects).
Keeping the string uncut and unstretched, carry it across to the second object and see whether it overshoots the top or falls short.

Compare each object to the same string and state the conclusion, voicing the transitive chain — e.g. 'this one is taller than the string; that one is shorter than the string; so this one is taller than that one.'
Try a second far-apart pair to transfer the idea.

Optional screen version: drag a fixed length of string to one tower, then carry it to the other and watch whether it overshoots or falls short, so the transitive step is something the child performs rather than is told.
activities.intendedInsight: A string kept at one fixed length can be carried to a place where two objects cannot meet, letting you decide which is longer by comparing each to the same intermediary.

activities.title: Building and extending a seriation staircase
feedback: If the child reorders only by trial and error, succeeds by luck, and cannot place a fourth ribbon: do not drill formal ordering rules or push insertion logic prematurely; give more compare-two experience and 'pick the shortest each time' prompts — a mental image of the series consolidates with age and working memory.
Probe: 'Where would a new, in-between ribbon go in your line? How did you decide?'
Confirm success when the child seriates by smallest-difference and can reliably insert new items.
activities.rationale: Serial ordering develops from trial-and-error toward a mental image of an increasing series; a shortest-first (then smallest-difference) strategy and insert-into-series tasks push beyond lucky guessing, and insertion logic draws on the same longer-than/shorter-than reasoning as transitivity.
sourceClaims: The Length Indirect Comparer compares two objects by representing them with a third object (e.g. a piece of string) and discussion focuses on transitive inference; a child at this level may use a ruler but often ignores the starting point. Serial Orderer levels: children first order 3–5 lengths by trial-and-error, then build a mental image of an increasing series and seriate by choosing the shortest then the 'smallest difference' next, and learn to insert a length by making it longer than those on one side and shorter than those on the other.
Year 2 pupils compare and order lengths and heights and use indirect comparison / a third object to compare objects that cannot be placed together.
learnerActions: Order three ribbons or cube-towers from shortest to longest using a strategy — pick the shortest, then the next shortest — rather than random swapping.
Progress to ordering five or more into an increasing 'staircase' where each step is the smallest available increase in length.
Check the finished line and fix any inversion (a shorter item placed after a longer one).

Take a new ribbon and decide where it belongs: it goes after every shorter ribbon and before every longer one, so it may land in between two ribbons or at either end if it is the shortest or longest of all.
Optional screen version: drag a fourth ribbon into a staircase that only settles when it sits above the shorter and below the longer neighbour, with a nudge when an inversion is left.
activities.intendedInsight: Transitivity becomes the rule that orders a whole set: when no two lengths are equal, each item is longer than everything before it and shorter than everything after, so a new item of a different length from all the others slots into exactly one place (if it matches an existing length, it can go right next to that item).

activities.title: Naming the transitive chain (check and consolidate)
feedback: Confirm a correct ordering and a correct spoken/selected answer; where the child answers the inference but cannot show it with objects, return to the string-carrying activity.
Use the staircase display only to summarise, then ask the child to re-derive the chain with real ribbons or string.
activities.rationale: An ordering step and a multiple-choice inference question match the ordering and transitivity evidence and are useful for checking understanding; a tap-to-reveal staircase can display and name the chain. These formats verify and consolidate but, on their own, elicit recognition rather than independent construction of the comparison.
sourceClaims: The Transitivity Principle — if A is longer than B and B is longer than C then A is longer than C — is a Grade 1 expectation used for indirect comparison when direct comparison is impossible; the canonical example is judging which of two paths is longer via a length of string laid along each (one path longer than the string, the other shorter).
learnerActions: Order a given set of ribbons shortest to longest as an ordering check.
Answer a transitive-inference question in words, e.g. 'The bookshelf is shorter than the string and the door is taller than the string — which is taller?'
Review a staircase display of the 'A > B > C, so A > C' chain, naming each term, as a summary reference after doing the hands-on work.
activities.intendedInsight: The transitive conclusion can be stated and recognised in words once it has been built through ordering and carrying an intermediary.

constraints: The learning objective is enactive: children must actually order objects and carry a constant intermediary, not only recognise or restate the rule. Recognition-only formats (choosing the taller from a worded prompt, tapping to reveal a chain) check or consolidate but do not elicit independent construction of the comparison.

A static staircase display can summarise and name the 'A>B>C so A>C' chain but does not let the child perform the ordering or the string comparison that carries the concept; use it as a reference, not the main activity.

The intermediary must be kept the SAME length throughout both comparisons — uncut, unstretched, aligned at the same starting end — or the comparison is invalid; this requirement is itself part of building conservation of length. Either approach is acceptable: a single fixed independent string compared to both objects, or a string set to one object's length then carried unchanged to the other; what is invalid is changing the string's length between the two comparisons.

Length comparison here is one-dimensional, so a flat staircase and a string are sufficient; a 3D spatial environment is not required for this objective (a scope note, not a claim that 3D can never aid any measurement learning).
Non-conservation of the intermediary and trial-and-error seriation are developmental stages, not errors to drill away; provide more experience rather than hard correction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the UK National Curriculum claim as verified:false; treat the Year 2 indirect-comparison statement as unconfirmed supporting context.

The original entry asserted that a conversation/Socratic format cannot teach this skill and that 3D 'adds no insight'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; softened to scoped scope notes. Talk can support the reasoning even though the core skill is enactive.

The original labelled recognition formats as able only to 'test rather than build' the reasoning; retained as an objective recognition-vs-construction limit, not as a claim that such formats have no instructional value.

Correction applied: the original screen-1 design and assess text described 'matching the string to the first object's height' (making them equal) while also voicing 'this one is taller than the string', which is internally inconsistent. Activity 1 now uses a fixed intermediate string compared to each object as the primary method, preserving the overshoot/fall-short observation and the transitive voicing.

Correction applied: an earlier wording ('do not re-size the string to match an object') over-restricted a valid technique. Representing one object with the string and carrying that fixed length is legitimate; the real requirement is that the string's length not change between the two comparisons. Constraints and Activity 1 now reflect this.

Self-audit: transitive logic (A>B and B>C implies A>C), the insert-into-series condition (longer than the item below, shorter than the item above), the string-as-constant-length requirement, and the 'bookshelf shorter / door taller than the string → door taller' inference were checked and are internally consistent; no arithmetic errors present in the retained content.

probeDeeper: How do you know this one is taller if you never put them next to each other?
If the string were longer than BOTH objects, could you still tell which is taller? How?
Where would a new, in-between ribbon go in your line? How did you decide?
I'll bend the string like this — is it still the same length? How could you check?
assess.correctAnswer: For the three ribbons, the child builds a correct series — selecting shortest then next-shortest, or checking and fixing inversions. For the two far-apart objects, the child uses the string as an intermediary: matches it to one object, keeps it uncut and aligned at the same end, carries it to the other, and states the conclusion — ideally voicing the transitive link ('this one is taller than the string, that one is shorter than it, so this one is taller').

errorPatterns.pattern: No transitive inference — pairwise only: sees the two far-apart objects as simply not comparable, or insists on carrying one object to the other, never using the string as a proxy for a length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model matching the string to A, then to B, and voice the chain 'A vs string, string vs B, so A vs B'; secure direct comparison first so the intermediary has something to stand for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the objects 'can't be compared, they're too far apart', or tries to move one object across; ignores the string as a stand-in.

errorPatterns.pattern: Trial-and-error seriation with no series image: orders three by random swapping, succeeds by luck, and cannot say where a new ribbon would be inserted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill formal ordering rules or push insertion logic prematurely; give more compare-two experience and 'pick the shortest each time' prompts — a mental image of the series consolidates with working memory and age.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reorders by trial and error, no shortest-first strategy; stuck when asked to insert a fourth ribbon.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not keep the intermediary constant: re-cuts, stretches, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons, so it no longer copies one fixed length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the string is a fixed copy of exactly one length; mark its end and align the same starting point for both objects before comparing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: String is stretched taut for one object and slack for the other, cut shorter, or measured from a different end each time.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation of the intermediary: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as carelessness — it is a conservation stage; straighten-and-compare so the child sees the length is preserved, and revisit later rather than correcting hard.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After the string is curved or repositioned, the child says 'it got shorter/longer' and re-judges.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot compare the far-apart pair (calls it impossible or tries to carry an object), or orders the three only by random trial with no reasoning offered.
responseLevels.full: Seriates by smallest-difference and inserts new items into the series, AND uses a constant intermediary to compare inaccessible objects, voicing the transitive inference and transferring it to a fresh case.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the string for one comparison OR orders the three correctly, but treats these as separate tricks — cannot articulate the transitive link, or orders three yet cannot reliably insert a fourth or transfer the string idea to a new far-apart pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give three ribbons of clearly different lengths and say 'Put these in order, shortest to longest.' Then point to a tall object by the door and another across the room that cannot be moved together, hand the child a piece of string, and say: 'Which one is taller? Show me how you can tell.' Watch what they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the concept reaches for the string as a stand-in and reasons through it; a child without it abandons the task as impossible, tries to eyeball or drag one object to the other, or re-cuts/stretches the string — each visibly different from correct transitive use. Ordering by shortest-first versus random swapping separates a mental image of an increasing series from lucky guessing.
